newsitem.title: CANADA: Thiessen says Canada stock market matches capacity.
newsitem.headline: Thiessen says Canada stock market matches capacity.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said strength in the Canadian stock market was consistent with the scope for expansion in an economy that was running below full capacity.

"The Americans have been operating essentially at full capacity for two or three years now. We still have yet to reach full capacity utilization," he said. "I think that really makes quite a difference, and that really means that there is an outlook in Canada for more expansion, and I think in these circumstances increases in the stock market of the sort we've had seem to be quite consistent with that."

Testifying before the Senate Banking Committee, Thiessen was asked about U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's concerns over possible irrational exuberance in stock markets, and whether central banks should comment on such issues.
"I don't think that it is the job of the central bank to make judgments about whether markets are somehow excessively exuberant or irrationally exuberant," Thiessen said.

"But I do know what Chairman Greenspan has been concerned about is a repeat of what happened in 1994...when indeed the Americans raised interest rates by one-quarter of one percent and there was an incredibly strong reaction in financial markets, particularly in the bond market, and that reverberated around the world," Thiessen said.
"It ended up I think having an excessive response to what was a gentle attempt to slow things down in the United States," he added.

Thiessen noted Canada's capacity for expansion made Canada's case different, but he added: "I wouldn't like, Mr. Chairman, to leave you with the impression that we at the central bank can make precise calculations about what is an appropriate stock market level, because of course we cannot."

He that in the 1970s and 1980s, an era of high inflation, a disproportionate amount of Canadians' savings were placed with banks in short-term deposits, and now this was rightly shifting to equities due to lower inflation and interest rates.
"I think it's terribly important that Canadians do become a source of equity financing for Canadian firms," he said.

"I guess I do rather hope is that in the mutual fund industry that there would be more of a realization than perhaps there has been in the recent past about savers who want to take risks and savers who don't want to take risks, and that there will be more of a sense of which sort of funds are minimal-risk funds and which ones aren't," Thiessen said.
"There's been more emphasis on high rates of return rather than on stability in rates of return."

"I think that's what Chairman Greenspan is worried about now, that somehow in the stock market there are expectations about the future which are just incredibly optimistic and which may not include in them the possibility of an increase in interest rates in the U.S.," Thiessen said.
"And I think it was more that kind of warning as opposed to an attempt to cause the stock market to move to a different level."
